If it replaces the struggle through which understanding is actually built, that's a loss we may not notice for years.

lines.speaker: Mr. Lindqvist
lines.text: I'd go further. The danger is precisely that the loss is invisible. Students produce polished answers, grades hold steady, and nobody can say what has quietly gone missing.

lines.speaker: Dr. Okafor
lines.text: Though I'd hate for that to become an argument for doing nothing. Students are using these tools already, whether we sanction it or not.

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.text: So what would responsible use look like?

lines.speaker: Mr. Lindqvist
lines.text: Assessment that rewards the process, not just the product: drafts, oral defences, explanations in the student's own words.

lines.speaker: Dr. Okafor
lines.text: And transparency. A tutor that cites its sources, as some now do, at least lets a student check whether an answer is grounded or merely plausible.

title: Is a kind lie still a lie?

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: Here's the case. A friend asks whether you liked the novel she spent five years writing. You found it tedious. Do you tell her?

lines.speaker: Minh
lines.text: I'd soften it, certainly. I'd praise what genuinely worked, the dialogue, say, and leave the rest unsaid.

lines.speaker: Clara
lines.text: But isn't leaving it unsaid just a lie by omission? If she's about to send it to publishers, my silence could cost her far more than my honesty would.

lines.speaker: Minh
lines.text: That assumes she's asking for an assessment. Half the time, the question is a request for reassurance, not a review.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: So the duty depends on what is really being asked, not on the literal words?

lines.speaker: Clara
lines.text: Partly. But we're rather quick to decide that other people want comfort, perhaps because comfort is what's easiest for us to give.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: A pointed observation. Hold on to it; it's exactly where Thursday's reading begins.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: You've written that the so-called replication crisis is, in a sense, good news. That sounds deliberately provocative.

lines.speaker: Professor Ilic
lines.text: Only slightly. When large projects tried to repeat well-known psychology experiments, a substantial share failed to produce the original results. That's uncomfortable, but discovering it is science working as intended.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Critics would say it shows that much of what was published simply wasn't true.

lines.speaker: Professor Ilic
lines.text: Some of it wasn't, certainly. But a failed replication doesn't prove the original effect was imaginary; it may have been smaller than claimed, or dependent on conditions no one recorded.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: So what has actually changed?

lines.speaker: Professor Ilic
lines.text: Quite a lot. Many journals now invite researchers to register their methods before collecting data, which makes it far harder to quietly adjust the analysis until something looks significant.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: And for the listener reading a headline about a surprising new study?

lines.speaker: Professor Ilic
lines.text: Treat a single study as an interesting rumour rather than a settled fact. Wait for it to be repeated, ideally by people with no stake in the result.
